A¶

A1. Clustering groups observations together and uses features without knowing the target labels. Examples in classification already have the right label, which lets it predict labels for new ones. Clustering algorithms include KMeans, DBSCAN and GaussianMixture.

A2. One use is clustering pixels, using their RGB values as the features. When pixels have a similar color, they end up in the same group. Another use is to measure the distance of each observation from one of the k centers after clustering. This gives each observation k new numbers, one per center, which can be used as features to predict something and validation data shows whether they help.

A3. An elbow plot graphs inertia against k. The elbow is the spot where the drop in inertia levels out as more centers are added. A silhouette score checks how well each point fits into its own group compared with the rest of the groups. A near 1 score means the groups are well separated and a higher average score helps show which k is better. The smallest inertia alone is not enough because inertia shrinks as k gets bigger and when every point has its own center, inertia reaches 0, which is not useful.

A4. In label propagation, you label one representative example from each group and then give that label to the rest of the group. An incorrect label can spread when a group is mixed because the items that don't match, like dog photos in a mostly cat group, get the representative's label, which is incorrect. To reduce this risk, you can check the results against genuinely labeled validation data to see whether the propagated labels are mostly right.

A5. Two methods that can handle large clustering datasets are mini-batch k-means and BIRCH. Two methods that use density are DBSCAN and Gaussian mixtures. One of the limitations of DBSCAN is that it can struggle if the density varies significantly across the clusters.

A6. One of the tasks is finding defective items on a production line from pictures, where labels begin to get expensive is when a human expert has to look at every picture and label it by hand, which takes time and costs money. I would ask a person to label the examples the model is most uncertain about. To check the new labels help, I would retrain the model and compare its results on labeled validation data.

A7. In outlier detection it doesn't assume the data is clean, because the training set may contain outliers. In novelty detection, the training set is assumed to be clean, so it has no outliers and only contains normal examples.

A8. The Gaussian mixture is a model that will assume the data comes from a mix of several Gaussian distributors. So for the clustering, you can use the predict_proba() to give each instance a probability for each cluster. For an anomaly detection, you can flag the instances located in low density regions.

A9. There are two approaches to choosing the number of components, comparing BIC values and using a Bayesian Gaussian mixture, which can shrink unnecessary weights. A low BIC means that the model is balancing how well it fits with how complex it is. It will not prove that the number of components will match the real-world categories.

A10. One k-means update by hand, with values 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 12 and starting centers 2 and 9.

Round 1, assign each value to its nearest center (starting centers 2 and 9):

value distance to 2 distance to 9 goes with
1 1 8 2
2 0 7 2
4 2 5 2
8 6 1 9
9 7 0 9
12 10 3 9

Updated centers (the mean of each group): 2.33 and 9.67.

Round 2, assign again with the updated centers:

value distance to 2.33 distance to 9.67 goes with changed?
1 1.33 8.67 2.33 no
2 0.33 7.67 2.33 no
4 1.67 5.67 2.33 no
8 5.67 1.67 9.67 no
9 6.67 0.67 9.67 no
12 9.67 2.33 9.67 no

No value changed groups after the update.

Inertia is the sum of the squared distances to each value's own center: 1.77 + 0.11 + 2.79 + 2.79 + 0.45 + 5.43 = 13.33.

Why six centers don't help: When you have six centers, every value gets its own center and that makes every distance 0 and the inertia is 0. That would not be a useful summary because each value would be in its own group, so nothing really grouped.

In [4]:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

results = []
for k in range(2, 9):
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(X_blobs)
    results.append({'k': k,
                    'inertia': model.inertia_,
                    'silhouette': silhouette_score(X_blobs, model.labels_)})

results_table = pd.DataFrame(results)
print(results_table.round(3))

I choose k=4. The inertia plot begins high drops steeply and then it flattens out at k=4, which is the elbow. The silhouette at its highest point is k=4 and goes down after that. This means that the groups are well separated at k=4. And both plots point to the same choice.

K-means divides the two crescents across both of the crescents because it groups by their distance to the nearest center.

In [9]:
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

x_limits = (X_moons[:, 0].min() - 0.15, X_moons[:, 0].max() + 0.15)
y_limits = (X_moons[:, 1].min() - 0.15, X_moons[:, 1].max() + 0.15)

dbscan_models = {}
for eps in (0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30):
    model = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=5).fit(X_moons)
    dbscan_models[eps] = model
    labels = model.labels_
    noise = labels == -1

    plt.scatter(X_moons[~noise, 0], X_moons[~noise, 1], c=labels[~noise], s=9)
    plt.scatter(X_moons[noise, 0], X_moons[noise, 1], c='gray', s=9, label='Noise')
    plt.xlim(x_limits)
    plt.ylim(y_limits)
    plt.title(f'DBSCAN eps={eps:.2f}')
    plt.xlabel('x1')
    plt.ylabel('x2')
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

The first graph has several grey points with about 7 colors. As the graphs progress, there are no more greys and two colors.

In [10]:
rows = []
for eps in (0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30):
    labels = dbscan_models[eps].labels_
    noise_count = int((labels == -1).sum())
    rows.append({'eps': eps,
                 'clusters': len(set(labels) - {-1}),
                 'noise_count': noise_count,
                 'noise_pct': 100 * noise_count / len(labels)})

dbscan_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(dbscan_table.round(2))

    eps  clusters  noise_count  noise_pct
0  0.05         7           77        7.7
1  0.10         2            1        0.1
2  0.20         2            0        0.0
3  0.30         2            0        0.0

As the eps increases, the number of clusters goes from seven down to two and the number of noise points goes down to zero. The groups that best follow the crescent shapes are eps=0.20 and eps=0.30, because they have two clusters one for each crescent and no noise. The crescents can be divided differently by K-means which groups by distance to the nearest center, cutting straight across curved shapes.

A noise label will not prove an observation is invalid, because it only means the point did not fit a cluster under the chosen eps and the min_samples settings. DBSCAN cannot call predict on new observations because scikit-learn’s DBSCAN does not have a predict method (it only has fit_predict).

While k increases from 10 to 50, the inertia goes down and the silhouette goes up. The silhouette scores are all close to 0, which means the groups overlap each other.

I had chose k = 50 because the silhouette score is highest on the table for k, even though the inertia keeps going down at every k.

for row, cluster_id in enumerate(show_clusters):

    for col in range(10):
        axes[row, col].axis('off')
        if col < len(members):
            axes[row, col].imshow(X_train[members[col]].reshape(64, 64), cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=1)
            axes[row, col].set_title(str(members[col]), fontsize=7)
fig.suptitle('Training faces from four clusters (titles are training-row numbers)')
plt.show()

Cluster 0 size 4 first row numbers [ 58 102 114 208]
Cluster 1 size 9 first row numbers [ 60  96  99 118 142 155 165 174 196]
Cluster 2 size 6 first row numbers [ 12  79 123 199 226 230]
Cluster 3 size 8 first row numbers [ 61  65  72  75  83 136 141 168]

Cluster 2 looks coherent because the faces look like the same person. Cluster 1 looks mixed because the faces have different lighting and head angles.

The clusters group faces by visual similarity, such as shadows, shapes, depth, color shades and expressions to name a few and not only by who the person is. The k does not have to equal 40 because clusters and identities answer different questions.

In [17]:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

raw_model = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=5000)
raw_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

raw_val_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_val, raw_model.predict(X_val))
print('Raw pixel validation accuracy:', raw_val_accuracy)

Raw pixel validation accuracy: 0.9625

The raw pixel baseline has a validation accuracy of 0.9625, which means 96 percent of the time it named the correct person.

In [18]:
d_train = {}
d_val = {}

for k in face_ks:
    d_train[k] = face_models[k].transform(X_train)
    d_val[k] = face_models[k].transform(X_val)

print(d_train[10].shape, d_val[10].shape)
print(d_train[50].shape, d_val[50].shape)

(240, 10) (80, 10)
(240, 50) (80, 50)

Transforming each photo with a k-means model gives the k distances per photo, one to each of the centers. For k = 10, the training distances have the shape of (240, 10).

In [19]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

distance_scalers = {}
distance_models = {}

for k in face_ks:
    scaler = StandardScaler().fit(d_train[k])
    clf = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=5000)
    clf.fit(scaler.transform(d_train[k]), y_train)
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_val, clf.predict(scaler.transform(d_val[k])))

    distance_scalers[k] = scaler
    distance_models[k] = clf
    print('k =', k, 'distance features, validation accuracy:', accuracy)

k = 10 distance features, validation accuracy: 0.6125
k = 20 distance features, validation accuracy: 0.8
k = 30 distance features, validation accuracy: 0.8375
k = 40 distance features, validation accuracy: 0.8625
k = 50 distance features, validation accuracy: 0.875

With the scaled distance features, the validation accuracy goes up as k goes up, from 0.6125 at k = 10 to 0.875 at k = 50. Every one of these is lower than the raw pixel baseline of 0.9625.

In [20]:
combined_scalers = {}
combined_models = {}

for k in face_ks:
    train_combined = np.column_stack([X_train, d_train[k]])
    val_combined = np.column_stack([X_val, d_val[k]])

    scaler = StandardScaler().fit(train_combined)
    clf = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=5000)
    clf.fit(scaler.transform(train_combined), y_train)
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_val, clf.predict(scaler.transform(val_combined)))

    combined_scalers[k] = scaler
    combined_models[k] = clf
    print('k =', k, 'pixels plus distances, validation accuracy:', accuracy)

k = 10 pixels plus distances, validation accuracy: 0.95
k = 20 pixels plus distances, validation accuracy: 0.95
k = 30 pixels plus distances, validation accuracy: 0.9625
k = 40 pixels plus distances, validation accuracy: 0.95
k = 50 pixels plus distances, validation accuracy: 0.95

With pixels plus distances, the validation accuracy was 0.95 for k = 10, 20, 40 and 50 as well as 0.9625 for k = 30. That is about the same as the raw pixel baseline of 0.9625. This experiment changes both the representation of pixels plus distances and the scaling with a new StandardScaler, compared with the raw-pixel baseline, so the comparison has to be read with care.

pixels_plus_distances 40.0      4136        0.9500
pixels_plus_distances 50.0      4146        0.9500

The table is comparing all 11 setups. The highest validation accuracy is 0.9625, which the raw pixels and the pixels plus distances at k = 30 have reached both. The distance-only features were lower, from 0.6125 at k = 10 to 0.875 at k = 50.

I choose the raw pixel classifier. It's tied with the pixels plus distances at k = 30 on validation accuracy (0.9625), so I picked the simpler representation, which takes fewer features and won't need a clustering step.

In [22]:
test_predictions = raw_model.predict(X_test)
test_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, test_predictions)

print('Test accuracy:', test_accuracy)
print('Correct predictions:', int((test_predictions == y_test).sum()), 'of', len(y_test))

Test accuracy: 0.95
Correct predictions: 76 of 80

I evaluated the selected raw pixel classifier on the 80 test photos one time. Its test accuracy was 0.95, with 76 of 80 predictions correct.

The cluster features were not able to clearly help. The distance-only features scored from 0.6125 to 0.875, this is below the raw pixel baseline of 0.9625 and the pixels plus distances scored 0.95 to 0.9625, which is about the same as the baseline. The k that looked best for clustering was k = 50, which had the highest silhouette score (0.171). The k that did best for classification was different, since the pixels plus distances did best at k = 30 (0.9625) and clusters and classification answer different questions. Windows showed a KMeans memory-leak warning and a joblib core-count warning while the models ran. I made no fix because they did not change the results.

I fit four Gaussian mixture models, with 1, 2, 5 and 10 components, on the PCA-reduced training faces. I used diagonal covariance because it will limit the number of parameters the model has to learn from this small dataset.

In [25]:
gm_rows = []
for n in (1, 2, 5, 10):
    gm_candidate = gm_models[n]
    gm_rows.append({'components': n,
                    'converged': gm_candidate.converged_,
                    'BIC': gm_candidate.bic(Z_train),
                    'AIC': gm_candidate.aic(Z_train)})

gm_table = pd.DataFrame(gm_rows)
print(gm_table.round(1))

converged_table = gm_table[gm_table.converged]
best_n = int(converged_table.loc[converged_table.BIC.idxmin(), 'components'])
gm = gm_models[best_n]
print('Selected components by lowest training BIC:', best_n)

   components  converged      BIC      AIC
0           1       True  26695.9  25470.7
1           2       True  26900.0  24446.2
2           5       True  30937.3  24797.4
3          10       True  38932.6  26649.5
Selected components by lowest training BIC: 1

I used the four Gaussian mixtures to compare them with BIC and AIC on the PCA-reduced training faces. All four of them converged. The lowest BIC was for the 1-component model, so I selected it as gm. A lower BIC balances fit against complexity, but it only says which model fits the training data best for its size. It can't prove the faces form real categories.

In [26]:
generated_Z, generated_components = gm.sample(12)
generated_pixels = pca.inverse_transform(generated_Z)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(12, 4))
for ax, pixels in zip(axes.ravel(), generated_pixels):
    ax.imshow(pixels.reshape(64, 64), cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.axis('off')
fig.suptitle('12 faces generated by the Gaussian mixture')
plt.show()

I generated 12 new faces by sampling from the selected 1-component Gaussian mixture and converting the samples back to pixels with the PCA’s inverse transform. The faces look blurry and distorted but are still recognizable as faces. They look this way because the model works on only 176 PCA numbers, so fine detail was already dropped. It also treats those numbers as independent, diagonal covariance and it draws random combinations that no real person has.

In [27]:
original_imgs = np.asarray(X_val)[:12].reshape(12, 64, 64).copy()

darkened_imgs = original_imgs * 0.5

val_original = original_imgs.reshape(12, 4096)
val_rotated = rotated_imgs.reshape(12, 4096)
val_flipped = flipped_imgs.reshape(12, 4096)
val_darkened = darkened_imgs.reshape(12, 4096)

print(val_original.shape, val_rotated.shape, val_flipped.shape, val_darkened.shape)

(12, 4096) (12, 4096) (12, 4096) (12, 4096)

I took the first 12 validation faces and kept an unchanged copy. I then made three modified versions of each that rotated 90 degrees, flipped left to right, and darkened by multiplying the pixel values by 0.5. I also changed the 64 × 64 pictures first and then flattened them again, so every group has the shape (12, 4096). These are synthetic test cases, not real defects, and they are kept separate from the training data.

I scored the 12 original validation faces and their three modified versions with the selected Gaussian mixture, using the existing PCA. The originals averaged -24.8. Test set, all 80 faces: proportion flagged at the frozen threshold of -65.2
      group  flagged  out of  proportion
0  original        4      80       0.050
1   rotated       80      80       1.000
2   flipped       11      80       0.138
3  darkened        0      80       0.000

I froze the model and the threshold at -65.2 and scored all 80 test faces and the same three modifications of them, without retuning anything. The threshold flagged 4 of 80 originals (0.050), all 80 rotated faces (1.000), 11 of 80 flipped faces (0.138) and none of the darkened faces (0.000). These modifications are synthetic test cases, not real defects.

The Gaussian mixture worked well for rotated faces. It flagged 11 of 12 on validation and all 80 on test, so a face turned on its side is very unusual to this model. It worked only partly for flipped faces, flagging 3 of 12 on validation and 11 of 80 on test. Most flipped faces still looked normal to the model, probably because a face is close to left-right symmetric. It failed completely for darkened faces, which were flagged 0 times on validation and test and their average log density was higher than the originals. I don’t know exactly why, but one possible reason is that halving the brightness moves the face closer to the model’s average in PCA space. That's just a guess I didn't test it. The modifications are synthetic test cases, not real defects and the flag rates are approximate, not guaranteed.

flipped (12, 4096) -> (12, 4096)

I reused the PCA fitted in C3 to reconstruct the faces. Each face was transformed into the PCA features and then converted back to 4096 pixels with inverse_transform. I did this for the 80 original validation faces and the three modified groups of 12 faces. I didn't clip the reconstructions.

original errors: (80,) average: 0.00225
rotated errors: (12,) average: 0.00811
flipped errors: (12,) average: 0.00304
darkened errors: (12,) average: 0.00097

I reconstructed each face with the PCA and computed one mean squared error per face, without clipping. The average error was 0.00225 for the 80 original validation faces, 0.00811 for rotated, 0.00304 for flipped and 0.00097 for darkened. A larger error means PCA rebuilt the face less well.

I showed the three validation faces next to their PCA reconstructions. The original face was rebuilt fairly closely, with some blur (error 0.00321). The rotated face with the highest error came back as a noisy, ghost-like upright face (error 0.01162), because PCA only keeps patterns from upright training faces. The darkened face with the highest error was rebuilt as a dim, blurry face that looks like its input (error 0.00124), so it stayed below the threshold and was the hardest case to flag.

In [37]:

    'group': test_flag_table['group'],
    'GMM flagged': test_flag_table['proportion'],
    'PCA error flagged': test_error_table['proportion']})

print('Test set, all 80 faces: proportion flagged by each method')
print(method_comparison.round(3))

Test set, all 80 faces: proportion flagged by each method
      group  GMM flagged  PCA error flagged
0  original        0.050               0.10
1   rotated        1.000               1.00
2   flipped        0.138               0.25
3  darkened        0.000               0.00

Both methods flagged all 80 rotated faces and none of the darkened faces. For flipped faces, the GMM flagged 0.138 and the PCA error flagged 0.25. The GMM flags faces with low log density as unusual and the PCA method flags faces with high reconstruction error as unusual. A modification that stays close to the PCA subspace can have a small reconstruction error, because PCA only measures how well a face can be rebuilt from the patterns it kept.

For compact groups, I would choose k-means, with the number of clusters chosen using the elbow and silhouette plots. Its limitation is that I have to choose k in advance. For curved groups, I would choose DBSCAN, because it found the two moons. Its limitation is that it depends on eps. At 0.05 it found 7 clusters and 77 noise points, while 0.10 to 0.30 found 2 clusters. For unusual face images, I would choose the Gaussian mixture on the PCA features. Its limitation is that it missed all of the darkened faces and most of the flipped faces on the test set.

Python 3.13.5, numpy 2.1.3, pandas 2.2.3, matplotlib 3.10.0 and scikit-learn 1.6.1. The random seed was 42 for the train/validation/test splits and for the Gaussian mixture. I made no changes to the suggested settings.
